    Foundations

    01

    Conjunctions at a glance

    What a conjunction does, and how the whole system fits together.

    A conjunction joins clauses (and sometimes smaller expressions) and shows the relationship between them. Some conjunctions join clauses of equal weight (and, but, or); others make one clause part of another (when, because, although, if). Some are made of two or more words: as soon as, in case, as long as.

    The conjunction map

    Open a branch, then select a conjunction to see its meaning, structure, example and typical error.

    Select a conjunction from the map.

    02

    How clauses connect

    Clause → conjunction → clause: the basic architecture of a complex sentence.

    Core idea

    A sentence can have more than one clause, usually joined by a conjunction which shows the relationship between them.

    I’ll phone youwhenI get home.
    It was getting lateandI was hungry.
    • We brought the food and they supplied the drink. addition
    • She was poor but she was happy. contrast
    • We can go swimming, or we could stay here. alternative
    • People disliked her because she was so rude. cause
    • I’ll phone you when I arrive. time

    Conjunction architecture

    Choose a relationship. The bridge changes shape to show how the two clauses are held together.

    Co-ordinate and subordinate clauses

    Co-ordinate clauses

    Co-ordinate clauses have equal weight: neither is part of the other.

    • Dan cooked supper and Joe washed the dishes.
    • The forecast was impressive but the results were disappointing.

    Examples: and, but, either … or.

    Subordinate clauses

    A subordinate clause with its conjunction is part of the main clause — for example its object or an adverbial.

    • I’ll phone you when I get home.
    • I told them that I knew nothing about it.

    Examples: when, after, how, that, as soon as, in case.

    Three kinds of subordinate clause

    For practical purposes, subordinate clauses fall into three groups. Each one can take the place of a simpler element in the main clause.

    Noun clause

    works like a noun phrase

    I told them a lie.

    I told them that I knew nothing about it.

    Adverbial clause

    works like an adverbial

    We drove home at high speed.

    We drove home as fast as we could.

    Relative clause

    works like an adjective

    She told me a funny story.

    She told me a story that made me laugh out loud.

    Coordination

    03

    Coordinating conjunctions

    Seven words that join grammatically equal parts: FANBOYS.

    Fforreason
    Aandaddition
    Nnornegative addition
    Bbutcontrast
    Ooralternative
    Yyetunexpected contrast
    Ssoresult
    Parallel structure

    A coordinating conjunction joins grammatically similar expressions: word + word, phrase + phrase, clause + clause. The two sides should match in form.

    • She is clever and hard-working. adjective + adjective
    • We can meet today or wait until Thursday. verb phrase + verb phrase
    • We waited indoors, for it was still raining. for = because; formal and literary
    • She trained for months, yet she still felt nervous. yet = but, stressing surprise
    • The printer was out of ink, so we emailed the handouts. result
    • She likes to swim and running. Unbalanced: use to swim and to run / swimming and running.
    04

    and, but, or

    Putting things together — from single words to complete clauses.

    and

    And can join two or more grammatically similar expressions, from single words up to complete clauses.

    • bread and cheese; the Prime Minister and his cabinet
    • You need to go home and have a good rest.
    • Her English is good and her Japanese is not bad.

    Lists

    With more than two expressions, we generally put and only before the last. In a very literary or poetic style and is sometimes left out, but this is unusual.

    • We drank, talked and danced.
    • He started as a cleaner, he worked his way up, and now he runs the company.
    • My dreams are full of darkness, despair, death. literary, unusual

    Repeated words

    In expressions joined by and, repeated words are often left out.

    • We need a saw, (a) hammer and (a) screwdriver.
    • She’s worked in China, (in) Thailand and (in) Brazil.

    Fixed expressions

    Some common expressions with and have a fixed order which cannot be changed. The shortest expression often comes first.

    bread and butter

    butter and bread

    hands and knees

    knees and hands

    thunder and lightning; knife and fork

    also: young and pretty, black and white, cup and saucer

    but

    But can also join grammatically similar expressions, although most often it joins clauses.

    • They were poor but happy.
    • There were some chairs but no tables.
    • We wanted to stay but we simply didn’t have time.
    • The film started well, but then it went downhill.

    or

    Or joins grammatically similar expressions. After a negative verb, we use or, not and. But or does not join negative adjectives or adverbs.

    • Would you like tea or coffee? We can meet today or wait until Thursday.
    • He doesn’t smoke or drink.
    • He doesn’t smoke and drink.
    • We were not comfortable or happy.
    • We were uncomfortable and unhappy.
    • We were uncomfortable or unhappy.
    Rulenot + verb/adjective … or
    CorrectIt’s not on the table or in the cupboard.
    Common errorIt’s not on the table and in the cupboard.
    Why?The single not applies to both places; and would suggest both at once.
    05

    Negative coordination

    not … or; not … nor; not … either; neither/nor + auxiliary; not … too.

    One not for two negative ideas

    When not (used once) refers to two or more verbs, nouns, adjectives, etc., we usually join them with or. We can use nor after a pause, to separate and emphasise a second verb, adjective, etc. Note that neither cannot be used in this way, and and cannot normally be used in this structure.

    • He doesn’t smoke or drink.
    • He doesn’t smoke nor drink.
    • She wasn’t angry or upset. It’s not on the table or in the cupboard.
    • Our main need is not food, nor money. It is education. nor after a pause, for emphasis
    • She didn’t phone that day, nor the next day.
    • The project was not successful in economic terms or in political terms.
    • The project was not successful in political terms and in economic terms.
    • The country suffered from a lack of employment legislation or of an independent labour union. also after negative nouns and adjectives; more normal than a lack of … and …

    Two separate negative clauses: not … either

    After a negative verb in one clause, we can add a second negative idea in another clause with not … either, or with neither/nor + be/auxiliary + subject. Also, as well and too are not normally used with not in this way.

    Jack isn’t hereeither|Neither/Nor+is / can / do+subject
    • Daniel isn’t here today. Jack isn’t here either.
    • Jack isn’t here neither.
    • Daniel isn’t here today. Neither is Jack.
    • I can’t sing, and nor can any of my family.
    • You can’t have an apple, and you can’t have an orange either.
    • … and you can’t have an orange also / as well / too.

    Positive + negative: not … also / as well / too

    After mentioning a positive fact or idea, we can add a negative point with not … also, not … as well or not … too.

    • You can have an apple, but you can’t have an orange too.
    • He drinks too much, but at least he doesn’t smoke as well.
    06

    Emphatic coordination

    both … and; either … or; neither … nor; not only … but also — giving both parts equal weight.

    both … and

    We often balance this structure, so that the same kind of words or expressions follow both and and. Unbalanced sentences are common, but some people prefer to avoid them. Both cannot begin a complete clause in this structure.

    bothprettyandclever— adjective ⟷ adjective
    • She’s both pretty and clever. adjectives
    • I spoke to both the Director and her secretary. nouns
    • She both dances and sings. verbs
    • She both dances and she sings. I both play the piano and the violin. unbalanced but common
    • He can both borrow the house and (he can) use the car.
    • Both he can borrow the house and he can use the car.

    either … or

    We use either … or to talk about a choice between two or more possibilities. We often balance the structure; unbalanced sentences are also common. Some books say either should not introduce more than two alternatives — this ‘rule’ is mistaken and does not correspond to normal usage.

    • I don’t speak either Russian or Polish.
    • You can have either tea or coffee. nouns
    • He’s either in London or in New York. prepositional phrases
    • Either you’ll leave this house or I’ll call the police. clauses
    • You can either have tea or coffee. You’ll either leave this house or I’ll call the police. unbalanced but common
    • If you want ice cream there’s either raspberry, lemon or vanilla.

    neither … nor

    The opposite of both … and; usually rather formal. It can connect more than two ideas. Neither cannot begin a complete clause in this structure. With two singular subjects, the verb is normally singular, but it can be plural in a less formal style.

    • I neither smoke nor drink. less formal: I don’t smoke or drink.
    • The film was neither well made nor well acted.
    • He neither smiled, spoke, nor looked at me.
    • Neither he smiled nor …
    • Neither James nor Virginia was at home. normal
    • Neither James nor Virginia were at home. less formal

    not only … but also

    In this rather formal structure, not only and but also go immediately before the expressions they modify. Mid-position with the verb is also possible. Not only can move to the beginning of a clause for emphasis; it is then followed by auxiliary + subject (do if there is no other auxiliary), and but can be left out.

    Not onlyhas / do / didshe / they… ;shehas also…
    • We go there not only in winter, but also in summer.
    • Not only the bathroom was flooded, but also the rest of the house.
    • The place was not only cold, but also damp.
    • She not only sings like an angel, but also dances divinely. mid-position
    • Not only has she been late three times; she has also done no work.
    • Not only do they need clothing, but they are also short of water.
    • Informal alternative: We don’t only go there in winter. We go in summer too.

    Subordination

    07

    Subordinating conjunctions

    Conjunctions that make one clause part of another.

    A subordinating conjunction introduces a clause that works inside the main clause. Many express time (when, after, before, while, until, as soon as), reason (because, as, since), condition (if, unless, as long as, provided), contrast (although, even though), precaution (in case) or comparison (as, as if, as though). Students whose first language joins clauses differently may find some of these patterns difficult — the modules that follow deal with each group in turn.

    08

    Contrast and concession

    although, though, even though, in spite of, despite.

    Situation. Last year Paul and Sarah had a holiday by the sea. It rained a lot, but they had a good time.

    • Although it rained a lot, they had a good time.
    • In spite of / Despite the rain, they had a good time.

    What follows each word?

    although+subject + verb→although it rained
    in spite of / despite+noun / pronounor-ing→despite the rain / being tired
    in spite of the fact (that) / despite the fact (that)+subject + verb
    despiteit was raining✗
    finite clausenoun phrase / pronoun-ing form

    although + subject + verb

    • Although it rained a lot, they had a good time.
    • I didn’t apply for the job although I had the necessary qualifications.

    although vs because

    • We went out although it was raining heavily. unexpected result
    • We didn’t go out because it was raining heavily. expected result

    in spite of / despite + noun, pronoun or -ing

    After in spite of or despite we use a noun, a pronoun (this / that / what etc.) or -ing. Despite means the same as in spite of, but it is used without of.

    • In spite of the rain, we had a good time.
    • She wasn’t well, but in spite of this she continued working.
    • In spite of what I said yesterday, I still love you.
    • I didn’t apply for the job in spite of having the necessary qualifications.
    • She wasn’t well, but despite this she continued working.
    • despite of this
    • I didn’t apply for the job in spite of the fact (that) / despite the fact (that) I had the necessary qualifications.

    in spite of vs because of

    • We went out in spite of the rain. (or … despite the rain)
    • We didn’t go out because of the rain.
    Rulealthough + clause; despite / in spite of + noun or -ing
    CorrectI couldn’t sleep although I was very tired / despite being very tired.
    Common errorI couldn’t sleep despite I was very tired. / In spite of the traffic was bad …
    Why?Despite and in spite of work like prepositions: they cannot take a subject + verb directly. Add the fact that if you need a clause.

    though and even though

    Though = although. In spoken English we often use though at the end of a sentence, meaning ‘but’. Even though (not even alone) is similar to although, but stronger.

    • I didn’t apply for the job though I had the necessary qualifications.
    • The house isn’t so nice. I like the garden though. = but I like the garden
    • I see them every day. I’ve never spoken to them though.
    • Even though I was really tired, I couldn’t sleep.
    • Even I was really tired, I couldn’t sleep.
    09

    Precaution: in case

    Doing something now because something might happen later.

    Your car should have a spare wheel in case you have a puncture (= because it is possible you will have a puncture). in case something happens = because it is possible it will happen.

    • I’d better write down my password in case I forget it.
    • Shall I draw a map for you in case you have a problem finding our house?
    • I’ll remind them about the meeting in case they’ve forgotten.
    • I don’t think it will rain, but I’ll take an umbrella just in case. just in case = for a smaller possibility
    • I’ll write down my password in case I will forget. We do not use will after in case.

    in case is not if

    We use in case to say why somebody does (or doesn’t do) something. You do something now in case something happens later.

    We’ll buy some more food in case Tom comes.

    buy food nowTom comes? (maybe)food ready either way

    We’ll buy some more food if Tom comes.

    Tom comes?only then: buy food

    in case

    • I’ll give you my phone number in case you need to contact me.
    • You should insure your bike in case it is stolen.

    if

    • You can call me on this number if you need to contact me.
    • You should inform the police if your bike is stolen.

    in case + past

    Use in case + past to say why somebody did something.

    • I gave him my phone number in case he needed to contact me.
    • I drew a map for Sarah in case she had a problem finding our house.
    • We rang the doorbell again in case they hadn’t heard it the first time.

    in case of + noun

    in case of = if there is … (especially on notices and instructions).

    • In case of fire, please leave the building as quickly as possible.
    • In case of emergency, call this number.
    10

    Conditions: unless, as long as, provided

    Exceptions and conditions, and the tense that follows them.

    unless = except if

    The club is for members only. You can’t go in unless you are a member. This means: you can’t go in except if you are a member; you can go in only if you are a member.

    • I’ll see you tomorrow unless I have to work late. except if I have to work late
    • There are no buses to the beach. Unless you have a car, it’s difficult to get there.
    • A: Shall I tell Lisa what happened? B: Not unless she asks you. tell her only if she asks you
    • Ben hates to complain. He wouldn’t complain about something unless it was really bad.
    • We can take a taxi to the restaurant — unless you’d prefer to walk.

    Instead of unless it is often possible to say if … not: Unless we leave now, we’ll be late. = If we don’t leave now, we’ll be late.

    unless and if … not: when do they overlap?

    Interchangeable

    When if not means ‘except if’ — a real exception to what is said:

    • Unless we leave now, we’ll be late.
    • If we don’t leave now, we’ll be late.

    Not a simple swap

    When the idea is not ‘except if’, unless sounds wrong. Test it by saying except if:

    • I’ll be surprised if he doesn’t come.
    • I’ll be surprised unless he comes. ‘I’ll be surprised except if he comes’ makes no sense.

    as long as / so long as and provided / providing

    As long as or so long as = if, on condition that. You can also say provided (that) or providing (that).

    • You can borrow my car as long as / so long as you promise not to drive too fast. This is a condition.
    • Travelling by car is convenient provided (that) / providing (that) you have somewhere to park. convenient, but only if you have somewhere to park
    • Providing (that) / Provided (that) the room is clean, I don’t mind which hotel we stay at.

    unless / as long as etc. for the future

    When talking about the future, we do not use will after unless / as long as / so long as / provided / providing. We use a present tense.

    • I’m not going out unless it stops raining.
    • unless it will stop
    • Providing the weather is good, we’re going to have a picnic tomorrow.
    • providing the weather will be good
    11

    The meanings of as

    as = at the same time as; as = because. Not every as means the same thing.

    as = at the same time as

    Use as when two things happen together at the same time, or to say that something happened in the middle of doing something else (often with the past continuous).

    • We all waved goodbye to Liz as she drove away. we waved and she drove away at the same time
    • As I walked along the street, I looked in the shop windows.
    • Can you turn off the light as you go out, please?
    • Kate slipped as she was getting off the bus. We met Paul as we were leaving the hotel.
    • Just as I sat down, the doorbell rang. just as = exactly at that moment
    • As the day went on, the weather got worse. I began to enjoy the job more as I got used to it. two changes over a longer period

    As I drove home, I listened to music. — same time

    driving homelistening to music

    When I got home, I had something to eat. — one after another (as I got home)

    got homeate

    as = because

    • As I was hungry, I decided to find somewhere to eat.
    • As it’s late and we’re tired, let’s get a taxi home. / Since it’s late and we’re tired, …
    • We watched TV all evening as we didn’t have anything better to do.
    • As I don’t watch TV any more, I gave my television to a friend of mine.

    as = because

    David wasn’t in the office as he was on holiday.

    As they lived near us, we used to see them quite often. (because they lived near us)

    when = time

    David lost his passport when he was on holiday. (during the time he was away)

    When they lived near us, we used to see them quite often. (at the time they lived near us)

    12

    like and as

    Similarity, manner and role.

    like+noun / pronounor-ing→ like a palace / like this / like walking on ice
    as+subject + verb→ as it was / as I showed you
    as+role / function→ as a photographer / as a place to visit

    like = similar to, the same as

    Here like is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun, a pronoun or -ing. Sometimes like = for example; you can also use such as.

    • What a beautiful house! It’s like a palace. not as a palace
    • Be careful! The floor has been polished. It’s like walking on ice.
    • It’s raining again. I hate weather like this.
    • ‘What’s that noise?’ ‘It sounds like a baby crying.’
    • I enjoy water sports, like / such as surfing, scuba diving and water-skiing.

    as = in the same way as, in the same condition as

    We use as with subject + verb. We also use like in this way. But with a noun or pronoun only like is possible.

    • I didn’t move anything. I left everything as it was / like it was.
    • You should have done it as I showed you / like I showed you.
    • You should have done it like this.
    • as this
    • You’re late as usual. As always, Nick was the first to complain.
    • Your phone is the same as mine.
    • the same like mine

    Other meanings of as + subject + verb

    • You can do as you like. do what you like They did as they promised.
    • As you know, it’s Emma’s birthday next week. Andy failed his driving test, as he expected.
    • As I said / Like I said yesterday, I’m sure we can solve the problem. like is not usual in these expressions, except with say

    as + noun: role, position, form

    As can also be a preposition (as + noun), but the meaning is different from like.

    as = in the position of

    As a taxi driver, I spend most of my working life in a car. (I am a taxi driver; it’s my job.)

    like = similar to

    Everyone in the family wants me to drive them to places. I’m like a taxi driver. (I’m not a taxi driver, but I’m like one.)

    • Many years ago I worked as a photographer.
    • Many words, for example ‘work’ and ‘rain’, can be used as verbs or nouns.
    • London is fine as a place to visit, but I wouldn’t like to live there.
    • The news of the tragedy came as a great shock.
    13

    like, as if, as though

    How somebody or something looks, sounds, feels or behaves — and imagined situations.

    look / sound / feel + like / as if / as though

    • That house looks like it’s going to fall down. / looks as if it’s going to fall down.
    • Amy sounded like / as if she had a cold, didn’t she?
    • I’ve just had a holiday, but I feel very tired. I don’t feel like / as if / as though I’ve had a holiday.

    look + adjective

    You look tired.

    look like / as if + subject + verb

    You look like you haven’t slept. / You look as if you haven’t slept.

    it looks like / it sounds like

    • Sarah is very late. It looks like / It looks as if she isn’t coming.
    • It looked like it was going to rain, so we took an umbrella.
    • The noise is very loud next door. It sounds like / as if / as though they’re having a party.

    With other verbs: how somebody does something

    • He ran like he was running for his life.
    • After the interruption, the speaker went on talking as if nothing had happened.
    • When I told them my plan, they looked at me as though I was mad.

    as if + past for an unreal present

    After as if we sometimes use the past when we are talking about the present. The meaning is not past: the past shows that the idea is not real. We use the past in the same way with if and wish. We do not normally use like in this way. You can use were instead of was.

    Patternas if + past = imagined, not real
    ExampleI don’t like him. He talks as if he knew everything.
    RealityHe does not know everything.
    Why past?The past tense marks distance from reality, not past time.
    • She’s always asking me to do things for her — as if I didn’t have enough to do already. I have enough to do already.
    • Joe’s only 40. Why do you talk about him as if he was / were an old man?
    • They treat me as if I were / was their own son. I’m not their son.
    14

    during, for, while

    When, how long, and at the same time as — three different structures.

    during + noun

    answers: when?

    duringthe movie

    I fell asleep during the movie.

    for + period of time

    answers: how long?

    fortwo hours

    We watched TV for two hours.

    while + subject + verb

    answers: at the same time as what?

    whileI was watching TV

    I fell asleep while I was watching TV.

    during

    during = at a time between the start and end of something. With time words (the morning, the night, the summer) you can usually say in or during.

    • We met some really nice people during our holiday.
    • The ground is wet. It must have rained during the night / in the night.
    • It’s lovely here during the summer / in the summer.

    for and during

    We use for (+ a period of time) to say how long. We do not use during to say how long: not ‘during two hours’.

    • Jess is going away for a week in September. I haven’t seen you for ages. Are you going away for the weekend?
    • It rained for three days without stopping.
    • during three days
    • ‘When did you fall asleep?’ ‘During the movie.’ — ‘How long were you asleep?’ ‘For half an hour.’

    during and while

    during + noun

    • I fell asleep during the movie.
    • We met a lot of interesting people during our holiday.
    • Robert suddenly began to feel ill during the exam.

    while + subject + verb

    • I fell asleep while I was watching TV.
    • We met a lot of interesting people while we were on holiday.
    • Robert suddenly began to feel ill while he was doing the exam.
    • We saw Clare while we were waiting for the bus.
    • While you were out, there was a phone call for you.
    • Alex read a book while Amy watched TV.

    while + present for the future

    When we are talking about the future, we use the present after while. Do not use will.

    • I’m going to Moscow next week. I hope the weather will be good while I’m there.
    • while I will be there
    • What are you going to do while you’re waiting?
    • while you’ll be waiting

    Advanced clause rules

    15

    Position of subordinate clauses

    First or last — depending on what you want to emphasise.

    Adverbial clauses can usually go first or last in a sentence, depending on the focus. Putting a clause at the end can give it more importance.

    Clause first

    While I was taking a shower, I slipped. emphasises what happened

    If you need help, just let me know.

    Although the bicycle was expensive, she decided to buy it.

    Because she was too angry to speak, Anna said nothing.

    Clause last

    I slipped while I was taking a shower. emphasises when it happened

    Just let me know if you need help.

    She decided to buy the bicycle although it was expensive.

    Anna said nothing, because she was too angry to speak.

    16

    Punctuation

    Commas with subordinate clauses.

    Commas are often used to separate longer or more complicated clauses. Shorter pairs of clauses are often connected without commas. When a subordinate clause begins a sentence, it is more often separated by a comma unless the sentence is very short.

    • They changed all their policies after they had won the election. short — no comma
    • They made a large number of disturbing changes in their policies, after they had won the election and settled in with a comfortable majority. long — comma
    • When we opened the door, we saw water running down the stairs. initial clause — comma
    • When we opened the door(,) we got a shock. very short — comma optional
    17

    Leaving words out

    What can disappear — and what must stay.

    Words for repeated ideas can often be left out in the second of two co-ordinate clauses, but not normally in a subordinate clause.

    Full form: She was depressed and she didn’t know what to do.
    ↓
    Reduced: She was depressed and didn’t know what to do. ✓ co-ordinate clause — the subject is recoverable
    Not possible: She was depressed, because didn’t know … — subordinate clause keeps its subject: because she didn’t know

    Reduced subordinate clauses

    After if, when, while, until, once, unless and (al)though, a pronoun subject and the verb be can often be dropped, especially in fixed expressions.

    • I’ll pay for you if necessary. = if it is necessary
    • If in doubt, wait and see. = if you are in doubt
    • When in Rome, do as the Romans do. Cook slowly until ready.
    • Once in bed, I read for twenty minutes and then turned out the light.

    Many time conjunctions (after, before, since, when, while, whenever, once, until) can be followed by -ing forms or past participles instead of a subject and full verb.

    • I always feel better after talking to you.
    • Some things are never forgotten, once learnt.
    18

    Special clause-joining patterns

    Separate sentences, one conjunction per link, relative pronouns, and wh-words after prepositions.

    Conjunctions in separate sentences

    Normally a conjunction connects two clauses into one sentence. However, a conjunction and its clause can stand alone — in answers, for emphasis, and in afterthoughts. The idea that a sentence must never begin with a conjunction is not correct: the structure is perfectly acceptable when used appropriately.

    • ‘When are you going to get up?’ ‘When I’m ready.’
    • ‘Why did you do that?’ ‘Because I felt like it.’
    • This government has got to go. Before it does any more damage. separated for emphasis
    • OK, I did it. — But I didn’t mean to. afterthought

    One conjunction for two clauses

    One conjunction is enough to join two clauses — we do not normally use two.

    Although she was tired but she went to work.

    Although she was tired, she went to work.

    She was tired but she went to work.

    Because I liked him, so I tried to help him.

    Because I liked him, I tried to help him.

    I liked him, so I tried to help him.

    As you know, that I work very hard.

    As you know, I work very hard.

    You know that I work very hard.

    However, we can use and or or together with a repeated conjunction.

    • We came back because we ran out of money, and because Anna got ill.
    • She didn’t write when I was ill, or when I got married.

    Relative pronouns

    Relative pronouns (who, which, that) also join clauses. A relative pronoun is the subject or object of the verb that comes after it, so we do not need another subject or object.

    • There’s the girl who works with my sister.
    • I’ve got a friend who works in a pub.
    • … who he works in a pub.
    • The man (that) she married was an old friend of mine.
    • The man that she married him …
    • She always thanks me for the money that I give her.
    • … the money that I give her it.

    who, which, what, etc. after prepositions

    Interrogative conjunctions like who, which, what, where, whether can follow prepositions. After common words like tell, ask, idea, prepositions are often dropped before these conjunctions. Prepositions are not normally used before that: either drop the preposition, or put the fact between the preposition and that.

    • We discussed the question of who to appoint as manager.
    • It depends on which day you are holding the meeting.
    • They were not at all interested in what I thought.
    • Tell me about your trip. BUT Tell me where you went.
    • Do you have any idea of the cost? BUT Do you have any idea what it costs?
    • I knew about his problems. BUT I knew that he had problems.
    • I knew about that he had problems.
    • I was not responsible for the fact that the documents were stolen.
    • I was not responsible for that the documents were stolen.
    19

    Tenses in subordinate clauses

    Why English says when I arrive, not when I will arrive — and when a future form is genuinely needed.

    Reasons for tense simplification

    If the main verb makes it clear what kind of time the speaker is talking about, it is not always necessary to show the same time again in the subordinate clause. Verbs in subordinate clauses are often simpler: present instead of future, simple past instead of would + infinitive, simple past instead of past perfect.

    Time shown in the subordinate clause

    This discovery means that we will spend less on food.

    It is unlikely that he will win.

    Time already shown by the main verb

    This discovery will mean that we spend less on food.

    I will pray that he wins.

    • You’ll find Coca-Cola wherever you go.
    • wherever you will go
    • He would never do anything that went against his conscience. more natural than … that would go …
    • I hadn’t understood what she said. more natural than … what she had said

    Present instead of future

    I’ll write to her when I have time.

    nowI have timeI write

    The main clause (I’ll write) already places everything in the future. Repeating will in the when-clause would add nothing, so English uses the simpler present.

    This happens after time conjunctions (when, until, after, before, as soon as) and in most other subordinate clauses: after if, whether, on condition that, after question words and relative pronouns, and in indirect speech.

    • I’ll write to her when I have time.
    • when I will have time
    • I’ll think of you when I’m lying on the beach.
    • when I will be lying
    • Will you stay here until the plane takes off?
    • It will be interesting to see whether he recognises you.
    • I’ll have a good time whether I win or lose. I’ll go where you go.
    • I’ll lend it to you on condition that you bring it back tomorrow.
    • He says he’ll give five pounds to anybody who finds his pen.
    • If she asks what I’m doing in her house, I’ll say I’m checking the gas.

    This also happens when the main verb is not future in form but refers to the future:

    • Phone me when you arrive. Make sure you come back soon.
    • You can tell who you like next week, but not until then.

    In comparisons with as and than, present and future verbs are both possible.

    • She’ll be on the same train as we are / will tomorrow.
    • We’ll get there sooner than you do / will.

    Present perfect for completion

    The present perfect is used instead of the future perfect to express the idea of completion.

    • I’ll phone you when I’ve finished.
    • when I will have finished
    • At the end of the year there will be an exam on everything you’ve studied.
    • everything you will have studied

    When the subordinate clause needs a future form

    A future verb is necessary in a subordinate clause if the main verb does not refer to the future (or to the same time in the future).

    • I don’t know where she will be tomorrow. main verb present: don’t know
    • I’m sure I won’t understand a word of the lecture.
    • I’ll hide it somewhere where he’ll never find it. two different future times
    • If she rings, I’ll tell her that I’ll ring back later. two different future times
    Key questionHas the main clause already fixed the future time?
    Yes → presentI’ll tell you when she arrives.
    No → futureI don’t know when she’ll arrive.
    Also futurewhen the subordinate event is at a different, later future time.

    in case, I hope, I bet, it doesn’t matter, etc.

    A present tense is normally used with future meaning after in case, even if the main verb is present or past. In an informal style, present verbs are often used with future meanings after I hope and I bet. Present tenses are also used with future reference after it doesn’t matter, I don’t care, I don’t mind, it’s not important and similar expressions.

    • I’ve got my tennis things in case we have time for a game tomorrow.
    • I hope you sleep well. I bet he gets married before the end of the year.
    • It doesn’t matter where we go this summer.
    • I don’t care what we have for dinner if I don’t have to cook it.
